patient.chief_complaint: New bilateral ptosis and diplopia attributed to possible MS relapse
patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on natalizumab presented for evaluation of new bilateral ptosis and diplopia over 6 weeks. She had been referred to the neurology clinic by her MS neurologist for evaluation of possible MS relapse. Her MS neurologist's concern was a new oculomotor finding on top of her prior documented internuclear ophthalmoplegia from an older right MLF lesion. The patient reports the bilateral eyelid drooping began approximately 6 weeks ago, initially intermittent and present mainly in the evenings. She noted double vision — horizontal, worsening on sustained upgaze — that was new and different from her chronic INO-related symptoms. Her MS neurologist had prescribed a 5-day course of high-dose IV methylprednisolone 2 weeks ago for presumed MS relapse. The ptosis and diplopia showed minimal improvement with steroids, which was unexpected for an acute MS relapse. She then began to notice mild fatigue when using her arms for overhead activities (hanging laundry, reaching for shelves) and mild difficulty chewing tough meats. She denied significant dysphagia. Her prior MS symptoms (right-sided hemiparesis, cerebellar ataxia, INO) are all at their chronic stable baseline. Repeat brain MRI performed 1 week ago for relapse evaluation showed no new or enhancing MS lesions. Anti-JC antibody index is elevated at 3.1 (high PML risk — she is on natalizumab extension beyond 24 months). Her MS neurologist noted the poor steroid response and the new neuromuscular features (jaw fatigue, arm fatigue) were atypical for an MS relapse and referred to general neurology for further evaluation. Anti-AChR antibodies have not been checked.

results.title: Concurrent MS and MG: case series and literature review
results.finding: MS and MG concurrent in <0.1% of patients but documented multiple times; natalizumab-associated MG cases reported (may trigger MG via immune reconstitution or altered B cell regulation); both conditions require separate targeted treatment; thymectomy for MG unaffected by MS

results.title: Natalizumab and autoimmune co-morbidities
results.finding: Natalizumab associated with paradoxical appearance or worsening of certain autoimmune conditions including MG; mechanism unclear but may involve peripheral B cell dysregulation from lymphocyte trapping in bone marrow

output.summary: Concurrent MS and MG is rare (<0.1%) but documented. Natalizumab has been associated with triggering or unmasking MG in some case reports. Both conditions require separate management. Thymectomy is still indicated for MG regardless of concurrent MS. Drug interaction between natalizumab and MG immunosuppression requires careful multidisciplinary coordination.
